questions.question:
**The question below consists of a set of labelled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.**

English may be a foreign

A-countries, but not for

B-those from India

C-language for students from other
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **CAB.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **The first part of the sequence should be C** as ‘English may be a foreign language…’ makes logical sense.
 
• **The next part that follows should be A**. ‘from other countries…’ is grammatically correct.
 
• If we use part B after C, ‘from other those…’ makes no sense.
 
• **Part B can end the sentence properly.**

Complete sentence__ – *English may be a foreign language for students from other countries, but not for those from India.*

Thus, the correct sequence is CAB, making **option 2** the correct answer.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select “no improvement”.**

A better example is a person who (has been assigned) the duty of planting trees and watering them along an expressway.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'No improvement'.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• The correct structure is:** *has been + verb in the past participle*.** It indicates that the action began in the past and continues in the present.

 
 
• ***Example**: She **has been considering** moving to another place.*
 
 
 
• The given sentence discusses a person whose job was assigned in the past and he still continues to perform that duty. So, no improvement is required, making **option 4 **the correct answer.
 
• Moreover, according to the **"Subject-Verb Agreement Rule"**, **'a person'** is a singular subject that will take a singular verb **'has' **with it
 
• *The correct sentence- A better example is a person who **has been assigned** the duty of planting trees and watering them along an expressway.*

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select “no improvement”.**

His friends claimed that he (been depressed) for a few months.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **had been depressed.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

The correct structure to be used: ***had been + verb in the past participle*.** This is used to indicate that the action began in the past and continued up to a given time in the past.

Let us see an example to understand:

__
 
• *I** had been worried** about you. Where were you all these days?*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

In the given sentence, the depression began in the past and he continued to be depressed for a period of time. That explains the use of ‘had been + verb’ structure. Now, the verb should be in the past participle. So, depressed is the correct form.

*His friends claimed that he **had been depressed** for a few months.*

Therefore, the correct answer is** option 2**.

questions.question: danger that ______ much knowledge
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** too.**

*Too *means excessively – it is used to stress the excessive degree of something.

Now, the question arises whether we should use too much or very much in the given sentence.

 
• ***Very much*** is used to mean to a great degree (but not excessive)

 
 
• Example: Your help is very much appreciated.
 
 
 
• ***Too much*** is often used to indicate more than what can be tolerated. (it often indicates unpleasantness)
 
 
• *Example : You are spending too much time on entertainment*
 
 

Here, in the given context, we are talking about *excessive *knowledge (highlighting some unpleasant aspect). So, *too much* is a proper fit.

*…danger that **too** much knowledge…*

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 2**.

questions.question:
**A sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect Speech. Out of the four given alternatives, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct Speech.**

He says, “Everybody is here.”

options.text: He says that everybody is here.
He says that everybody was here.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **He says that everybody is here.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• In Direct speech, the message is conveyed in the words of the speaker.
 
• In Indirect speech, the message is reported in our words. 
 
• When we convert Direct speech to Indirect speech, we omit the quotation marks (“…”). Also, the conjunction *that *is added before introducing the words spoken between quotation marks. So, we can eliminate option 1.
 
• If the reporting verb is in the present tense, the verb in the reported speech does not undergo any change during transformation. The reported speech is conveyed as it had been originally in direct speech.
 
 
• Keeping these points in mind, the sentence in Indirect Speech becomes: *He says that everybody is here*
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 2**.

questions.question:
**A sentence has been given in Active/Passive Voice. Out of the four given alternatives, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active Voice.**

Somebody has stolen my mobile phone.

options.text: My mobile phone had been stolen.
My mobile phone has been stolen.
My mobile phone will be stolen.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **My mobile phone has been stolen.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• The subject is someone that works on the object.
 
• A sentence is said to be in Active Voice when the subject performs the action
 
• When the subject is being acted upon by the verb – it is Passive Voice.
 
• The sequence in Active voice – Subject + verb + object
 
• The sequence in Passive voice – Object + verb + Subject
 
• The meaning conveyed by the sentence in both voices will remain the same. Only the sequence of the subject and the object (or the action) changes.
 
• Let us understand this through an example
 
 
• Active Voice: ‘She eats an apple every day’
 
• Passive Voice : ‘An apple is eaten by her every day’
 
 
 
• Note that *eats* changes to *is eaten. **We always change the main verb form to the past participle form of the verb***
 
 
• The given sentence is in Active Voice as *somebody* is the subject performing an action of stealing. The sentence when converted in Passive voice becomes: *My mobile phone has been stolen (has *changes to *has been*). **'Somebody' which is missing in the passive voice is an inferred object of the passive voice sentence. **
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 2**.

questions.question:
**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select ‘No Error’.**

We can make donations to NGOs (1)/that are engaged in planting trees, (2)/or in anyway work towards saving the environment. (3)/No error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **3- the error lies in only Part 3.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in part 3 of the sentence, making **option 3** the correct answer.
 
• The word **anyway** means: in spite of something that has been mentioned before.
 
 
• Example: It was raining heavily, but we drove to the mall** anyway**.
 
 
 
• * ***Any** means one or some of a thing.
 
 
• Example: Do you have **any** food left?
 
 
 
• The speaker here refers to any work towards saving the environment.
 
• There is no point to highlight in spite o__f in the given sentence. So, the use of **any way** is incorrect.
 
• **Hence, the correct sentence is:** *We can make donations to NGOs that are engaged in planting trees or in **any work** towards saving the environment.*
